Class EngineEventBridge

java.lang.Object
de.hallerweb.enterprise.prioritize.service.process.EngineEventBridge
@Component public class EngineEventBridge extends Object
The outbound bridge: the one place where a domain event reaches into a running BPMN process. It turns NfcScannedEvent and TelemetryThresholdEvent into a Flowable message so a process that was waiting for that real-world signal can continue.

Orchestration, not ownership (the line held throughout the Flowable work): the bridge only wakes a process that already chose to wait. Nothing here starts a process, owns a lifecycle, or changes platform state — remove Flowable and the events simply have one listener fewer.

One correlation rule. An event carries a resourceId; a waiting instance states which resource it waits for in a process variable named "awaitedResourceId". Correlation is exactly the pair (message name, awaited resource id) — deliberately not the business key, which already answers "what is this instance about" (project:/task:) and must not be overloaded. A BPMN author writes: 

<intermediateCatchEvent id="awaitScan">
  <messageEventDefinition messageRef="nfcScan"/>
</intermediateCatchEvent>
with nfcScan declared as a <message name="nfcScan"/>, and sets awaitedResourceId to the resource being watched (e.g. from a start variable). The resource id is compared numerically, so it does not matter whether the author typed it as a Long, an Integer or a numeric String — the single most common way this kind of correlation silently fails.

Fan-out to all matching instances. A resource may legitimately feed several processes at once (an inspection round and an alarm escalation, say), so the message is delivered to every waiting execution whose awaited resource matches, not just one.

After commit, in a fresh transaction, best effort. Like the MQTT bridges, delivery is handled AFTER_COMMIT so only persisted signals propagate, and a delivery failure is logged, never propagated back to the already-committed source operation. Each messageEventReceived is wrapped in its own Spring transaction: the woken process runs on synchronously and may reach back into the platform through the facade (create a task, store a document), and those JPA writes must share one committing transaction with the engine's own — without it the process advances but its platform effects are silently lost (the AFTER_COMMIT phase has no active transaction of its own). One transaction per instance also keeps the failure isolation: one instance rolling back does not drag the others down.

  • Method Details

    • onNfcScan

      @TransactionalEventListener(phase=AFTER_COMMIT) public void onNfcScan(NfcScannedEvent event)
      Wakes every process instance that waits (on "nfcScan") for the resource this tag sits on, injecting the scan's context as process variables so the diagram can react to it. A scan that nobody waits for is a normal no-op.

    • onTelemetryThreshold

      @TransactionalEventListener(phase=AFTER_COMMIT) public void onTelemetryThreshold(TelemetryThresholdEvent event)
      Wakes every process instance that waits (on "telemetryThreshold") for the resource whose telemetry rule just changed state, injecting the transition (new state, value, data point, severity) so the diagram can branch on it. Fired only on the OK↔ALARM flank, so a woken process reacts to a real change, not to every reading.
